blocks.text: The same aluminium housing can be cast in sand for very little tooling and a rough finish, or in a hardened steel die at six figures of tooling and a finish you can almost anodise straight away. Neither is the right answer in general: the right answer depends on how many parts you need, how accurate they must be, and what alloy they are made of.

blocks.markdown: **Casting** shapes a part by pouring liquid metal into a mould cavity and letting it solidify. Three processes cover most production. In **sand casting** the mould is packed from sand with a binder around a pattern, used once and broken up to remove the part. In **investment casting** (lost wax) a wax pattern is coated with ceramic slurry, the wax is melted out and metal is poured into the hot ceramic shell, which is broken away. In **high-pressure die casting (HPDC)** molten metal, usually a low-melting alloy such as aluminium, zinc or magnesium, is injected under high pressure into a reusable steel die and solidifies in seconds.

blocks.title: Process capability
blocks.text: Process capability means the tolerance and surface finish a process can hold routinely, together with the sizes, alloys and volumes it suits. Values depend on part size and care, so the table gives typical orders of magnitude only.

rows: Almost any, including iron and steel
Almost any, including stainless steel and superalloys
blocks.caption: Typical process capabilities (orders of magnitude, not guarantees)

blocks.markdown: The economics follow from tooling and unit cost. If the tooling cost is $T$ (spread over $N$ parts) and the per-part cost excluding tooling is $u$, then the cost per part is $c=T/N+u$. A process with high $T$ but low $u$ only wins at high volume. The following illustrative figures (not market data) show the pattern.

blocks.title: Choosing by annual quantity
blocks.prompt: For a small aluminium housing the illustrative costs are: sand casting $T=3000$, $u=9.00$; investment casting $T=12000$, $u=6.50$; die casting $T=90000$, $u=1.80$ (currency units). Find the cheapest capable process at $N=500$, $5000$ and $100000$ parts.

steps.latex: Sand 15.00, investment 30.50, die casting 181.80, so sand casting is cheapest.
Sand 9.60, investment 8.90, die casting 19.80, so investment casting is cheapest.
Sand 9.03, investment 6.62, die casting 2.70, so die casting is cheapest.

blocks.answer: Sand casting wins at 500 parts, investment at 5000, die casting at 100000; tolerance and finish needs must also be checked.

blocks.title: Selecting on geometry and specification
blocks.prompt: A stainless steel valve body of 1.5 kg needs $\pm0.3$ mm on the seat region and $R_a\le3\ \mu$m, with 2000 parts per year. Select a casting process.

steps.text: Material rules out HPDC: stainless steel melts far above the temperature at which steel dies survive, and die casting is for low-melting non-ferrous alloys.
Tolerance and finish of $\pm0.3$ mm and $3\ \mu$m exceed what sand casting normally holds (typical $\pm1$ mm or worse, $R_a$ above 6 $\mu$m).
Investment casting meets tolerance, finish and alloy, and its tooling cost is acceptable at 2000 per year.

blocks.answer: Investment casting is the appropriate process.

blocks.markdown: Casting defects arise from how the metal fills and freezes. **Gas porosity** is rounded cavities from dissolved gas (for example hydrogen in aluminium, whose solubility drops sharply on freezing) or from air trapped by turbulent filling and mould gases that cannot escape. **Shrinkage cavities** are irregular voids formed in the last region to freeze when liquid cannot feed the volume contraction, usually from an undersized riser, hot spots or poor feeding paths. A **cold shut** is a seam where two streams of metal meet without fusing because the first has partly frozen or is covered by an oxide skin, caused by low pouring temperature, slow pouring, thin sections or long flow paths. A related defect is the **misrun**, an incompletely filled cavity.

rows: Smooth, round holes, often near the surface
Dissolved gas, trapped air, wet sand, poor venting
Degas the melt, dry moulds, vent, reduce turbulence
Rough, irregular void in thick sections
Inadequate feeding; undersized riser or hot spot
Line or seam where flows meet
Low metal temperature, slow pour, thin wall, poor gating
Raise pouring temperature, thicker walls, better gating
blocks.caption: Defects and their remedies

blocks.title: Match the process to the whole specification
blocks.text: Check in this order: alloy compatibility, size, tolerance and finish, then annual volume and tooling cost. A process that fails on alloy or tolerance is out regardless of cost.

blocks.title: Cost figures are illustrative
blocks.text: The numbers in the cost examples are chosen to show the pattern of tooling versus volume. A real selection needs quotations and also considers lead time, post-machining and quality.

points: Sand casting is cheap in tooling and flexible but rough; investment casting gives fine tolerance in many alloys; HPDC gives fast, accurate parts in low-melting alloys at high tooling cost.
Cost per part is $T/N+u$, so high-tooling processes only win at high volume.
Gas porosity, shrinkage cavities and cold shuts have distinct causes: trapped or dissolved gas, poor feeding, and failure of streams to fuse.
Process selection must satisfy alloy, size, tolerance, finish and volume together.

questions.stem: Which casting process is the most economical choice for 500 000 thin-walled aluminium electronic housings a year with $\pm0.2$ mm tolerance?

options.text: Sand casting
High-pressure die casting
Investment casting
Hand-packed green sand casting

distractorRationale.a: Sand casting cannot hold $\pm0.2$ mm on thin walls and has high unit cost per part.
distractorRationale.c: Investment casting can hold the tolerance but its slow, labour-intensive unit cost is not justified at this volume.
distractorRationale.d: Hand-packed sand casting is the least accurate and slowest of all.

questions.explanation: HPDC combines a fast cycle, thin walls and good tolerance for low-melting alloys, so its high tooling cost is spread across a large volume. The other processes cost far more per part at this scale.

questions.stem: A casting shows a thin seam on its surface where two streams of metal met but did not fuse. What is this defect and its most likely cause?

options.text: Shrinkage cavity, caused by an undersized riser
Gas porosity, caused by dissolved hydrogen
Hot tear, caused by pouring too fast
Cold shut, caused by metal that was too cold or poured too slowly

questions.correctOptionText: Cold shut, caused by metal that was too cold or poured too slowly

distractorRationale.a: A shrinkage cavity is an internal irregular void in a late-freezing region, not a surface seam.
distractorRationale.b: Gas porosity gives round holes, not seams.
distractorRationale.c: Hot tears are cracks from restrained contraction; the description is of unfused metal streams.

questions.explanation: A cold shut is a seam where two metal fronts meet after one has partly frozen or oxidised. It is promoted by low pouring temperature, slow filling, thin sections and long flow paths.

questions.stem: A cast aluminium part shows small smooth round holes distributed through the section, with the melt known to be saturated with hydrogen. What is the most likely mechanism and cure?

options.text: Gas porosity from hydrogen rejected during freezing; degas the melt
Shrinkage porosity from undersized riser; add a riser
Cold shut from low pouring temperature; raise temperature
Misrun from low fluidity; thicken the wall

questions.correctOptionText: Gas porosity from hydrogen rejected during freezing; degas the melt

distractorRationale.b: Shrinkage voids are angular or irregular and appear in thick last-to-freeze regions rather than as smooth round holes.
distractorRationale.c: Cold shuts are seams, not holes.
distractorRationale.d: A misrun is an incomplete filling of the cavity, not internal holes.

questions.explanation: Hydrogen is far more soluble in liquid aluminium than in solid, so it comes out of solution as the metal freezes and forms rounded pores. Degassing the melt and drying the mould materials removes the source.

questions.stem: A 25 kg ductile iron pump casing is needed in a quantity of 200 per year with a tolerance of about $\pm2$ mm and $R_a$ of 12 $\mu$m. Which process is most suitable?

options.text: High-pressure die casting
Investment casting
Sand casting
Hot rolling

distractorRationale.a: HPDC is limited to low-melting non-ferrous alloys and its tooling could not be justified at this volume.
distractorRationale.b: Investment casting is capable but needlessly expensive for the loose tolerance and size.
distractorRationale.d: Rolling does not produce a hollow pump casing.

questions.explanation: Iron, a large size and a loose tolerance at low volume point to sand casting. The tooling is just a pattern, and the rough finish can be accepted or machined where needed.

questions.stem: A 0.2 kg precision part in 17-4 PH stainless steel needs $\pm0.15$ mm and a smooth surface at 20 000 parts per year. A colleague proposes die casting to save unit cost. What is your recommendation?

options.text: Use die casting with a long-life steel die
Use sand casting, since the part is small
Use die casting, but pour at a lower temperature
Use investment casting, since die casting is not suited to stainless steel

questions.correctOptionText: Use investment casting, since die casting is not suited to stainless steel

distractorRationale.a: Steel dies are not used for stainless steel because it melts far above the temperature at which the die steel survives repeated contact.
distractorRationale.b: Sand casting cannot hold $\pm0.15$ mm and gives a rough finish.
distractorRationale.c: Lowering the pouring temperature cannot change the melting point of the alloy and would cause misruns.

questions.explanation: HPDC is restricted to low-melting alloys because the die would be destroyed by molten steel. Investment casting holds fine tolerance in stainless steel and 20 000 per year is a reasonable volume for it.

questions.stem: A die costs 60 000 currency units and each part costs 1.20 units to make excluding tooling. Calculate the total cost per part, in currency units, when 40 000 parts are made.
questions.explanation: The tooling per part is $60000/40000=1.50$, so the total cost is $1.50+1.20=2.70$ per part. At low volumes the tooling term would dominate.

questions.stem: Sand casting needs tooling of 2500 units and costs 11.00 units per part. Die casting needs tooling of 45 000 units and costs 2.50 units per part. Calculate the annual quantity at which the two processes have equal total cost.
questions.explanation: Setting $2500+11N=45000+2.5N$ gives $8.5N=42500$ and so $N=5000$ parts. Below this, sand casting is cheaper; above it, die casting is.

questions.stem: A two-cavity die casting machine has a cycle time of 45 s per shot (two parts per shot). It runs 8 h per day for 250 days per year with 85 percent availability. Calculate the number of parts it can make in a year.
questions.explanation: Shots per day $=8\times3600/45=640$, giving 1280 parts per day. Over 250 days that is 320 000 and with 85 percent availability the capacity is $272000$ parts, so the machine easily meets volumes of 100 000 or more.

questions.stem: Compare sand, investment and high-pressure die casting for a part that may be needed in either 200 or 200 000 units. Discuss tolerance, finish, tooling cost and unit cost, and state which you would choose at each volume for an aluminium part.
markingGuide: Sand: loose tolerance and rough finish, lowest tooling cost
Investment: fine tolerance and finish, medium tooling, higher unit cost
HPDC: fine tolerance, thin walls, very high tooling but lowest unit cost
Cost per part is $T/N+u$ so tooling is amortised over volume
200 units: sand or investment depending on spec; 200 000 units: HPDC
questions.explanation: At 200 units tooling dominates so sand or investment casting is chosen. At 200 000 units the low unit cost of HPDC repays its tooling, provided the alloy is low-melting.

questions.stem: A batch of aluminium castings is rejected for three problems: (i) rounded pores throughout, (ii) an internal rough cavity beneath a thick boss, (iii) a seam in a thin wall far from the gate. Name each defect, give the most likely cause and propose a process change for each.
markingGuide: (i) Gas porosity: dissolved hydrogen or trapped air; degas, dry the mould and vent, reduce turbulence
(ii) Shrinkage cavity: inadequate feeding of the last-to-freeze boss; larger riser, chill or redesign
(iii) Cold shut: metal front partly frozen or oxidised before meeting; raise pouring temperature, speed up fill, improve gating, thicken wall
Distinguishes smooth round (gas) from rough irregular (shrinkage) voids
Links causes to filling and freezing behaviour
questions.explanation: Each defect has a signature: smooth round pores indicate gas, rough internal cavities indicate lack of feed, and seams indicate unfused flow fronts. The remedies follow from those causes.
